blocks.html: Searching means finding whether a particular value, called the key, is present in a collection of data, and if it is, finding where.

items.html: Successful search: the key is found, and we report its position (index).
Unsuccessful search: the whole collection has been checked and the key is not there. In C++ we usually return −1 to mean "not found", because −1 can never be an array index.
Finding your roll number on the result notice board.
Looking up a word in a dictionary.
Finding a contact on your phone.
Searching for a patient's record by registration number at a clinic.
Google Search, which finds pages among billions in a fraction of a second.

blocks.html: This chapter covers three methods: linear search (check one by one), binary search (halve the list every time, on sorted data only), and hashing (jump almost straight to the answer).
Idea: Start at the first element and compare each element with the key, one by one, until the key is found or the list ends. It is also called sequential search. The list does not need to be sorted.

blocks.html: The work grows in direct proportion to n, so linear search is O(n). For 10 lakh records, the worst case is 10 lakh comparisons.
When to use linear search: for small lists, for unsorted data, for data that changes all the time, or when you need every match and not just the first one.
Idea: This method works only on sorted data. Look at the middle element:

items.html: if it equals the key, the search is over;
if the key is smaller, it can only be in the left half, so throw away the right half;
if the key is larger, it can only be in the right half, so throw away the left half.

blocks.html: Every comparison removes half of the remaining elements. This is how you find a word in a dictionary: open it in the middle, decide whether the word comes before or after that page, and repeat on the half that is left.

items.html: low = 0 , high = n - 1 .
While low <= high :
mid = low + (high - low) / 2
If arr[mid] == key , return mid.
Else if key < arr[mid] , set high = mid - 1 (search the left half).
Else set low = mid + 1 (search the right half).
Return −1 (not found).

blocks.html: Why low + (high - low) / 2 instead of (low + high) / 2 ? For very large arrays, low + high can be more than the largest int value and overflow. Both formulas give the same answer, but the first one is always safe.

blocks.html: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem. Binary search fits this naturally: searching the whole array becomes searching one half.
Each recursive call is placed on the function call stack (Chapter 3). The base case low > high stops the recursion.

Each step halves the range. Starting with n elements, after k steps only n / 2ᵏ elements are left. The search ends when one element is left, so k is about log₂ n. The maximum number of comparisons is ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1, which makes binary search O(log n).
In a sorted list of 100 crore Aadhaar-style numbers, binary search needs at most 30 comparisons.

items.html: The data must be sorted first, and sorting takes time (Chapter 5).
It needs direct access to the middle element, so it suits arrays and vectors but not linked lists.
If the data changes often, keeping it sorted is extra work.

blocks.html: Linear search checks items one by one. Binary search halves the list every time. Hashing tries to go straight to the right place in one step.
Think of a school with 10 classrooms numbered 0 to 9, where each student sits in the room given by the last digit of their roll number. To find roll number 47, you go directly to room
7. You do not search the whole school.

items.html: A hash table is an array of slots (also called buckets).
A hash function turns a key into a slot number. The most common one for integers is the remainder method:

blocks.html: Example: table size = 10, keys = 34, 16, 2, 93, 80
To search for 93, calculate 93 % 10 = 3 and look in slot 3. It is found in one comparison.
To search for 55, calculate 55 % 10 = 5. Slot 5 is empty, so 55 is not present. Again, one comparison.
Now insert 43. Since 43 % 10 = 3, it needs slot 3, but slot 3 already holds 93. When two keys get the same slot, it is called a collision. There are two common fixes.

(a) Linear probing (open addressing): if the slot is full, try the next slot (3 → 4 → 5 ...), wrapping round to 0 after the last slot, until an empty one is found. For 43: slot 3 is full (93), slot 4 is full (34), slot 5 is empty, so 43 goes into slot 5. To search for 43 later, follow the same path: 3, 4, 5, found.

blocks.caption: Figure 6.3 · hash table of size 10, with one collision solved by linear probing

blocks.html: (b) Chaining: each slot holds a small list. Both 93 and 43 are stored in slot 3's list.

rows: A list in the same slot

blocks.html: A good hash function spreads keys evenly, so collisions are rare and the search stays very close to one step: O(1) on average.
C++ has ready-made hash tables: unordered_set (stores keys) and unordered_map (stores key–value pairs). They handle the hash function and collisions for you.

items.html: Searching finds whether a key is present and where. An unsuccessful search usually returns −1.
Linear search checks elements one by one. It works on unsorted data and is O(n): 1 comparison at best and n at worst.

Binary search works only on sorted data with direct access. It compares the key with the middle element and throws away half the range each time. It is O(log n), with at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 comparisons.
Use mid = low + (high - low) / 2 to avoid overflow. Binary search can be written with a loop or with recursion.
Hashing uses a hash function such as key % size to compute the slot of a key in a hash table, giving O(1) average search.
A collision happens when two keys get the same slot. Two fixes are linear probing (try the next slot) and chaining (a list in each slot).
